codex.summary: Dominant AI-compute vendor: GPUs plus the interconnect (NVLink/NVSwitch) and rack designs (HGX, MGX/NVL) around them.
codex.explain: NVIDIA sells the reference platforms - HGX boards and full NVL racks - while ODMs assemble variants, which is why every competitor defines themselves against its fabric and software. CUDA maturity is the moat the numbers in this game reflect.
tradeoffs: Best software and fabric, highest prices, tightest allocation in shortages

codex.summary: Volume ODM/whitebox builder: first to market with NVIDIA HGX and AMD UBB server chassis.
codex.explain: Supermicro's business is packaging other vendors' silicon into every cooling and rack flavor (air, DLC, ORv3) fast. Buying the board from NVIDIA and the box from Supermicro is the classic AI-cluster recipe.
tradeoffs: Speed and breadth of catalog versus thinner own-IP and support bench

codex.summary: Taiwanese ODM offering aggressive alternates to Supermicro, especially G-series GPU servers.
codex.explain: GIGABYTE's G493-class boxes host 8 OAM AMD accelerators and often undercut rivals on price. Its liquid-cooled variants were early to the 1kW-per-GPU era.
tradeoffs: Cost-competitive second source for UBB servers
Support and firmware polish trail the tier-1s

codex.summary: Tier-1 enterprise server vendor: PowerEdge head nodes, storage, and integration muscle.
codex.explain: Dell (like HPE) sells the whole stack to enterprises - GPU servers, PowerScale/APEX storage, financing - and its IR7000 rack is its NVL72 vehicle. Enterprises pay the Dell premium for one throat to choke.
tradeoffs: Enterprise SLAs and global spares at a price premium over whitebox

codex.summary: RISC-V AI-hardware startup whose Wormhole/Blackhole chips and Galaxy servers mesh over plain Ethernet.
codex.explain: Tenstorrent bets that Ethernet-native scale-up plus open-source tooling (TT-Metalium) can undercut proprietary fabrics. Its hardware is cheap per FLOP; the ecosystem is the risk you underwrite.
tradeoffs: Very low cost and no fabric tax; immature software stack

codex.summary: Wafer-scale computing vendor: the CS-3 appliance trains and serves models on a single dinner-plate chip.
codex.explain: Cerebras sidesteps multi-GPU sharding entirely - one WSE-3, weights streamed from MemoryX, clusters of up to 2048 systems. Buyers get extreme simplicity per system at a bespoke price.
tradeoffs: Deterministic scaling and blistering decode; single-vendor lock and few ports

codex.summary: Incumbent CPU giant whose Gaudi accelerators bet against proprietary scale-up fabrics.
codex.explain: Gaudi 3 systems use integrated RoCE Ethernet for both scale-up and scale-out, riding Intel's Xeon installed base and Tofino-era networking DNA. After the 2024 wind-down toward Gaudi 3 as the last of the line, software continuity moved to the Habana-to-LPU transition.
tradeoffs: Xeon ubiquity and open fabrics; Gaudi roadmap risk

codex.summary: The assembler behind much of the world's servers, including NVIDIA MGX racks for GB200 NVL72.
codex.explain: Foxconn (Hon Hai) builds to others' specs at hyperscale margins; its MGX rack is the physical skeleton NVL72 ships in. Buying racks from the ODM avoids brand markup but puts integration QA on you.
tradeoffs: Scale pricing and early availability on hot designs
Thin direct support; you or an integrator handle integration

codex.summary: Not a company but the Open Compute Project: the ORv3 rack and OAM specs that hyperscalers publish for everyone.
codex.explain: OCP specs let any fabricator build standards-compliant racks, power shelves and accelerator modules, which is how AMD's UBB ecosystem exists. "Buying OCP" means buying spec-compliant gear from the open market.
tradeoffs: Standards kill vendor lock-in; community support only, no SLA

codex.summary: The spot market: commodity racks, JBODs, DRAM and SSDs with no brand behind them.
codex.explain: Generic gear fills the unglamorous layers - warm storage, head-node scratch, spare DIMMs - where specs are standardized and the premium brands add little. Lead times are short because no allocation queue applies.
tradeoffs: Cheap and available; weak RMA and firmware support when it breaks

codex.summary: World's largest memory and enterprise-SSD maker: DRAM, HBM, and PM/BM-series NVMe.
codex.explain: Samsung's PM9A3/PM1743 SSDs are the default enterprise flash, and its DRAM rides in nearly every server. Memory pricing cycles (shortages and gluts) show up in this game as its price drift.
tradeoffs: Top reliability and availability at mid-premium prices

codex.summary: US-headquartered memory vendor: DDR5 RDIMMs, MRDIMMs, and 9400/9550 datacenter SSDs.
codex.explain: Micron pushes the performance edges - MRDIMM buffered modules and mixed-workload Gen5 flash - and is the second source that keeps Samsung honest on price. Its 9550 targets AI read/write mixtures specifically.
tradeoffs: Often first with new module technologies
Second-source volumes can lag Samsung's in shortages

codex.summary: Korean memory maker, the dominant supplier of HBM for AI accelerators and a top DDR5 vendor.
codex.explain: Every MI- and H-series GPU depends on SK hynix (and Micron/Samsung) HBM3e supply; its DDR5 RDIMMs including the popular 96GB hybrid-die parts fill server channels. HBM allocation squeezes are the hidden bottleneck of GPU ramps.
tradeoffs: HBM leadership makes it a strategic supplier
Consumer-market swings whipsaw its DRAM pricing

codex.summary: High-performance storage vendor whose A3I appliances are the reference file tier for DGX SuperPODs.
codex.explain: DDN built its name on Lustre-parallel scratch for HPC and now sells AI400X2-class NVMe systems tuned for checkpoint floods and GPU-direct reads. When a 100k-GPU run must restart in minutes, this is what writes the checkpoint.
tradeoffs: Top sustained throughput per U; appliance pricing hurts $/PB

codex.summary: Software-defined parallel filesystem vendor tuned for GPU clusters.
codex.explain: WEKA runs on commodity NVMe servers and exposes a POSIX namespace over RDMA, feeding GPUs hundreds of GB/s. You license the software per capacity and own the hardware choices.
tradeoffs: Software licence is a recurring cost

codex.summary: Software-defined unstructured-storage vendor selling one namespace that spans NVMe performance nodes to capacity boxes.
codex.explain: VAST's CNode/DBox split decouples performance from capacity, serving S3 and NFS from the same datastore - a popular simplification for AI data lakes. Disaggregated shared-nothing architecture is the pitch; simplicity of one system is what buyers notice.
tradeoffs: One namespace for hot and cold data
Performance per node is modest - scale horizontally

codex.summary: The challenger compute platform: Instinct MI accelerators, EPYC server CPUs, and Pensando DPUs/NICs under one roof.
codex.explain: AMD is the only credible end-to-end alternative to NVIDIA - EPYC hosts every HGX box anyway, Instinct MI300X-class parts beat NVIDIA on HBM capacity per dollar, and Pensando supplies the networking. The catch is ROCm software maturity, which the sim reflects as a sub-1.0 software multiplier.
tradeoffs: More HBM and FLOPs per dollar than NVIDIA; thinner software ecosystem
Open ecosystem intent (UALink, OAM) versus shipping volume today

codex.summary: Inference specialist: the LPU (Language Processing Unit), a deterministic SRAM-only processor that keeps whole model weights on-chip.
codex.explain: Groq removes HBM entirely - 230MB of on-die SRAM and a statically scheduled pipeline mean no branch mispredictions, no cache misses, and extraordinary tokens-per-second at excellent latency. The price is tiny per-chip capacity, so big models need hundreds of LPUs in lockstep, and it serves inference only, not training.
tradeoffs: Massive tokens/s and p95 latency wins on supported models
SRAM-only: hundreds of chips per model, specialist capacity only

codex.summary: Merchant switch-silicon king: Tomahawk and Jericho ASICs that power most of the Ethernet switches in this catalog.
codex.explain: Broadcom does not sell you a switch - it sells the silicon inside Arista, Cisco, Celestica and whitebox boxes. Tomahawk 5 (51.2T) and Tomahawk 6 (102.4T) define the price-performance curve of scale-out fabrics, and its Jericho line adds deep buffering for AI congestion.
tradeoffs: Commodity economics: every vendor competes on the same silicon
Feature differentiation lives in software, so vendor choice still matters

codex.summary: The datacenter Ethernet leader: EOS-based leaf/spine and AI-backend switches built on Broadcom silicon.
codex.explain: Arista took the hyperscaler playbook - single EOS image, deep telemetry (CloudVision) - and became the default AI fabric vendor for Ethernet backends. Its 7800R4 and 7060X6 lines target exactly the 400/800G leaf-spine tiers this game wires.
tradeoffs: Best-in-class EOS software and support at a premium over whitebox
Rides Broadcom silicon, so ASIC features arrive on Broadcom's schedule

codex.summary: The networking incumbent, entering AI fabrics with Silicon One-based Nexus/8000-series Ethernet switches.
codex.explain: Cisco's answer to Arista in AI is its own Silicon One G100/G200 ASICs plus the enterprise service machine - the largest support organization in networking. Enterprises already standardized on Cisco optics, ops tooling and TAC; AI backends are the new battleground.
tradeoffs: Unmatched global support and enterprise integration
Silicon One is newer to AI-scale backends than Tomahawk incumbency

codex.summary: Power-management heavyweight: pad-mount transformers, switchgear, and the 93PM-series UPS feeding AI halls.
codex.explain: Eaton is one of the few vendors spanning medium-voltage utility gear down to rack PDUs, which is what a facility build actually sequences: transformer, switchgear, UPS, busway. Its 93PM UPS (up to 1.5MW per frame) and 99% eco-mode efficiency are the workhorses behind many AI sites.
tradeoffs: Full MV-to-rack power chain from one vendor simplifies commissioning
Lead times on transformers and switchgear are the facility critical path

codex.summary: Datacenter infrastructure generalist: APC UPS/PDUs, EcoStruxure monitoring, Uniflair CRAHs and CDUs under one controls umbrella.
codex.explain: Schneider sells the facility as a system - power (Galaxy VX/VS UPS), white-space cooling, and the EcoStruxure software that ties them together. For AI retrofits its RDHx (passive rear-door) line is the classic way to squeeze ~2x density out of an air hall.
tradeoffs: Integrated monitoring and global service coverage
Generalist depth: specialist AI vendors (CDU/immersion) out-feature it at the edge cases

codex.summary: The datacenter power-and-cooling pure-play: Liebert UPS, power shelves, CRAHs, chillers and the CDUs behind most NVL-class deployments.
codex.explain: Vertiv sits at the center of the liquid-cooling gold rush - its 230V/415V AC and 48V DC power chain plus XDU/xCDU family (800kW-2.3MW liquid-to-liquid and liquid-to-air) is the reference path for GB200 racks. When an AI hall is specified, Vertiv is usually in the RFQ.
tradeoffs: Broadest AI-era power+cooling portfolio and field service network
Premium pricing; hot new CDU capacity is allocation-constrained like GPUs

codex.summary: Taiwanese power specialist: PSUs and power shelves inside half the industry's servers, plus busway, CDUs and fan coils.
codex.explain: Delta is the silent incumbent of the power layer - its 97%+ efficiency rectifiers populate OCP power shelves and its liquid components (CDUs, manifolds, cold plates) ride the same ODM supply chains that build AI trays. Buying Delta means hyperscaler economics at the component level.
tradeoffs: OEM pricing and 97-98% conversion efficiency at the shelf
Component-grade support: no white-glove facility service like Vertiv

codex.summary: Direct-to-chip liquid cooling specialist: cold plates and rack/inline CDUs shipping inside most HGX and UBB liquid servers.
codex.explain: CoolIT pioneered production GPU cold plates (A100-era) and now sells both the plate side (cold plates on every SXM module) and the facility side (CHx CDUs up to MW class, liquid-to-liquid and liquid-to-air). If a tray needs 8 cold plates, odds are they are CoolIT or an ODM badge on the same designs.
tradeoffs: Deep cold-plate expertise and GPU-vendor co-design
Rack-scale CDU redundancy (n+1 pumps) must be designed in, not assumed

codex.summary: Facility-scale liquid cooling specialist: CDUs, coolant distribution units and rear-door heat exchangers for AI halls.
codex.explain: Motivair builds the big liquid-to-liquid CDUs (up to ~2.3MW) and facility side loops that sit between chillers and the rack manifolds of NVL72-class deployments. In 2025 Schneider took a majority stake - a signal that facility liquid is the growth tier of cooling.
tradeoffs: Facility-grade CDU engineering with true concurrent maintainability
Facility side only: you still need plate-level vendors inside the trays

codex.summary: Immersion-cooling pioneer: single-phase immersion tanks and the coolant-handling ecosystem (baths, CDUs, fluids) around them.
codex.explain: Submer drops whole servers into tanks of dielectric oil - single-phase immersion that removes fans entirely and enables 100kW+ per tank. It sidesteps leak anxiety of DLC but demands oil-compatible hardware (no thermal paste washout, buoyancy-aware boards) and tank-scale service workflows.
tradeoffs: Highest density and PUE floor; no water anywhere near electronics
Immersion-branded hardware, awkward RMA flow - every service is a lift-and-drain
